content: The Doctor of Chiropractic (DC or DCM) is an academic degree specifically designed for chiropractic physicians. In the United States, this degree is classified as a first professional degree. Chiropractic physicians are legally recognized as physicians by the U.S. Federal Government, the Joint Commission (which amended its rules in 2009 to include DCs), and the laws of most states, with notable exceptions being New York and California, likely due to historical American Medical Association (AMA) politics. The term physician is legally regulated, similar to terms like university or bank, and its use is determined by legislative bodies rather than professional associations. Chiropractic physicians are licensed healthcare professionals authorized to diagnose and treat human illnesses. They conduct comprehensive physical, orthopedic, and neurological examinations, take and interpret their own X-rays, and order and analyze laboratory tests. Based on these evaluations, they determine whether a patient’s condition falls within their scope of practice. If the condition is outside their expertise, they are trained to refer the patient to another type of doctor. Although they do not prescribe legend drugs or perform surgery, chiropractic physicians are considered primary care doctors. This designation is due to their role as a portal of entry into the healthcare system, meaning patients can seek their care without a referral. Chiropractic is a healthcare profession focused on diagnosing, treating, and preventing mechanical disorders of the musculoskeletal system and understanding how these disorders affect the nervous system and overall health. The practice emphasizes manual treatments, particularly spinal manipulation and adjustments. By restoring normal function to the musculoskeletal system, chiropractors aim to alleviate disorders and associated pain or discomfort caused by accidents, stress, poor posture, lack of exercise, illness, or daily wear and tear. Chiropractors adopt a holistic approach to health, considering physical, psychological, and social factors in their care. The Doctor of Chiropractic degree originated with Daniel David Palmer, the founder of chiropractic, who began awarding the degree to students completing his short instructional courses. Palmer, who was self-taught and not medically educated, conferred the degree upon himself and his students. Over time, the profession has continued to grant this degree to graduates of chiropractic schools in the U.S. and Canada. In 1966, the U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare initially classified the degree as spurious, but its status was later revised, and it is now recognized among other doctoral degrees. Chiropractic physicians are considered primary healthcare providers in the U.S. and Canada, meaning patients can directly access their services without a referral. In the United States, chiropractors are trained in accredited chiropractic schools overseen by the Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE). To obtain licensure, graduates must pass four examinations administered by the National Board of Chiropractic Examiners and meet state-specific requirements. Most state boards require at least two years of undergraduate education, with an increasing number mandating a four-year bachelor’s degree. All licensing boards require completion of a four-year program at an accredited chiropractic college leading to the DC degree. Once licensed, chiropractors in most states must complete 12–50 hours of continuing education annually. Chiropractic colleges also offer postdoctoral training in specialties such as neurology, orthopedics, sports injuries, nutrition, rehabilitation, industrial consulting, radiology, family practice, pediatrics, and applied chiropractic sciences. After completing such training, chiropractors may take examinations to achieve diplomate status in specific specialties, including orthopedics, neurology, and radiology. Chiropractic programs require at least 4,200 hours of combined classroom, laboratory, and clinical experience. The final two years of training emphasize courses in manipulation, spinal adjustment, and clinical experience in physical and laboratory diagnosis, orthopedics, neurology, geriatrics, physiotherapy, and nutrition.
